analysis.one_liner: Exempts refineries using hydrofluoric acid from having to evaluate safer alternative technologies.
analysis.headline: The House Energy and Commerce Committee advanced the bill 26–19, but the full House never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Refineries use hydrofluoric acid to make gasoline; if the acid escapes, it can form a toxic vapor cloud. Under current EPA rules, those refineries must include in their hazard assessments an evaluation of safer technologies and alternative safeguards. This bill would erase that requirement for any refinery that holds a Clean Air Act permit or promises to follow Recommended Practice 751, a guidance document written by the oil industry's own trade association. The bill cleared committee but never reached the House floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners and operators of refineries that use hydrofluoric acid alkylation units. They would no longer be required by EPA rules to analyze safer alternatives — such as switching to a different acid or modified technology — potentially avoiding large capital costs and preserving their existing process equipment.

how_it_helps.text: Eliminates the federal requirement that refineries with hydrofluoric acid alkylation units include an assessment of safer technology and alternative risk management measures in their hazard assessments.

Lets a refinery qualify for the exemption either by holding a construction or operating permit under the Clean Air Act, or by demonstrating conformance with American Petroleum Institute Recommended Practice 751, an industry guidance document.
The bill's stated purpose is to 'prohibit the phase out of gasoline and prevent higher prices for consumers,' framing the exemption as protecting gasoline supply and prices.

analysis.who_pays: People who live and work near refineries using hydrofluoric acid. If an accidental release occurs, the chemical can form a toxic vapor cloud, and the public would lose the mandated evaluation of whether safer technology could reduce that risk. Communities near refineries bear the added accident risk; taxpayers fund EPA's Risk Management program either way.

drawbacks.text: Hydrofluoric acid is hazardous and corrosive, and an accidental release can form a toxic vapor cloud that threatens people far beyond the plant fence line; the bill removes the one requirement that forces operators to formally weigh safer alternatives.

The alternative compliance path relies on American Petroleum Institute Recommended Practice 751, guidance written by the industry's own trade association, so a self-authored industry standard would substitute for the EPA hazard-assessment requirement.

Supporters would argue the exemption protects gasoline production capacity and consumer prices; the honest cost is that neighbors of refineries lose a layer of analysis designed to identify safer processes, and the bill offers no independent verification beyond the industry guidance document.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer-price framing in the bill's title is not matched by any consumer provision; the bill's concrete effect is regulatory relief for refinery operators. The benefit to operators is avoiding the cost of studying and potentially adopting safer alkylation technology. The cost is concentrated on fence-line communities and workers, who would face the same accident risk without the mandated search for safer alternatives. The public gets nothing in exchange.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared committee and was placed on the House calendar, but House leadership never brought it up for a floor vote, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Dan Crenshaw introduced the bill on February 24, 2023, with five original Republican cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
The Subcommittee on Environment, Manufacturing, and Critical Metals considered and marked up the bill on February 28, 2023, forwarding it to the full committee by a vote of 10–6.
The full Energy and Commerce Committee ordered the bill reported by a vote of 26–19 on March 9, 2023, and reported it on March 23, 2023 as H. Rept. 118-13.
The bill was placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 6, meaning it was eligible for consideration by the full House, but no floor vote ever occurred.
The bill received no action in the Senate and never became law before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Residents and workers near refineries using hydrofluoric acid came out ahead: the existing requirement that operators evaluate safer technologies and alternative safeguards stays in place because the bill never became law. Refinery operators gained nothing but also lost nothing, keeping the status quo.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and the bill advanced through subcommittee (10–6) and committee (26–19) on near-party-line votes; no Senate sponsor ever signed on.

industries.note: The bill would exempt refineries with hydrofluoric acid alkylation units from the EPA requirement to evaluate safer technologies, sparing operators the potential cost of studying or adopting less dangerous acid processes. The savings accrue to the industry while the accident risk of a toxic vapor cloud remains with nearby residents.

The bill lets a refinery qualify for the exemption by conforming to Recommended Practice 751, guidance written by the industry's own trade association, making an industry-drafted standard a substitute for the EPA hazard-assessment requirement and locking in industry self-policing.
